etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English parcel, from Old French parcelle (“a small piece or part, a parcel, a particle”), from Late Latin particella, diminutive of Latin particula (“particle”), diminutive of partem (“part, piece”). Doublet of particle.

quote.citation: 1892, Walter Besant, chapter II, in The Ivory Gate […], New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: At twilight in the summer […] the mice come out. They […] eat the luncheon crumbs. Mr. Checkly, for instance, always brought his dinner in a paper parcel in his coat-tail pocket, and ate it when so disposed, sprinkling crumbs lavishly […] on the floor.

quote.citation: 1904–1905, Baroness Orczy [i.e., Emma Orczy], “The Lisson Grove Mystery”, in The Case of Miss Elliott, London: T[homas] Fisher Unwin, published 1905, →OCLC; republished as popular edition, London: Greening & Co., 1909, OCLC 11192831, quoted in The Case of Miss Elliott (ebook no. 2000141h.html), Australia: Project Gutenberg of Australia, February 2020:
quote.text: “H'm !” he said, “so, so—it is a tragedy in a prologue and three acts. I am going down this afternoon to see the curtain fall for the third time on what  […]  will prove a good burlesque ; but it all began dramatically enough. It was last Saturday  […]  that two boys, playing in the little spinney just outside Wembley Park Station, came across three large parcels done up in American cloth.  […] ”

definitions.definition: An individual consignment of cargo for shipment, regardless of size and form.
An individual item appearing on an invoice or receipt (only in the phrase bill of parcels).
A division of land bought and sold as a unit.
An indiscriminate or indefinite number, measure, or quantity; a collection; a group.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: […]  this youthful parcel / Of noble bachelors stand at my bestowing,

quote.citation: 1847 March 30, Herman Melville, chapter 2, in Omoo: A Narrative of Adventures in the South Seas; […], London: John Murray, […], →OCLC, page 79:
quote.text: […]  instead of sitting (as she ought to have done) by her good father and mother, she must needs run up into the gallery, and sit with a parcel of giddy creatures of her own age  […]

definitions.definition: A small amount of food that has been wrapped up, for example a pastry.
A portion of anything taken separately; a fragment of a whole; a part.

quote.citation: 1731, John Arbuthnot, chapter 4, in An essay concerning the nature of aliments‎[1], London: J. Tonson, page 85:
quote.text: The same Experiments succeed on two Parcels of the White of an Egg  […]

quote.citation: 1881, John Addington Symonds, The Renaissance in Italy, Volume 5, Part I, New York: Henry Holt, Chapter 1, p. 2,[2]
quote.text: The parcels of the nation adopted different forms of self-government, sought divers foreign alliances.

quote.citation: 1982 April 3, “Mousie Mousie Wildflower”, in Gay Community News, page 15:
quote.text: I don't think we are sitting pretty / So far away from our fair city / But I love you more than any parcel of earth.

definitions.definition: To wrap something up into the form of a package.
To wrap a strip around the end of a rope.
To divide and distribute by parts or portions; often with off, out or into.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Their woes are parcell’d, mine are general.

quote.citation: 1665 (first performance), John Dryden, The Indian Emperour, or, The Conquest of Mexico by the Spaniards. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for H[enry] Herringman […], published 1667, →OCLC, Act I, scene ii, page 12:
quote.text: Thoſe ghoſtly Kings would parcel out my pow’r, / And all the fatneſs of my Land devour;

quote.citation: 1806, [Thomas Maurice], Indian Antiquities: Or, Dissertations Relative to the Antient Geographical Divisions,  […]  of Hindostan:  […] , volume I. Containing the Dissertation on the Antient Geographical Divisions of Hindostan, London: Printed  […]  by C. & W. Galabin  […]  and sold by John White  […] , pages 231–232:
quote.text: Hindostan was then parcelled out into twelve grand divisions, called soobahs, to each of which a viceroy was assigned, by the title of Soobahdar, corruptly written Soobah by European writers; for, soobah signifies province: many of these soobahs were in extent equal to large European kingdoms.

quote.citation: 1864, Alfred, Lord Tennyson, “Aylmer’s Field”, in Enoch Arden, etc.‎[3], London: Edward Moxon, pages 94–95:
quote.text: Then the great Hall was wholly broken down, / And the broad woodland parcell’d into farms;

definitions.definition: To add a parcel or item to; to itemize.

quote.citation: c. 1606–1607 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Anthonie and Cleopatra”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: […]  that mine own servant should / Parcel the sum of my disgraces by / Addition of his envy!

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Part or half; in part; partially.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Second Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: Thou didst swear to me upon a parcel-gilt goblet  […]

quote.citation: 1826, [Walter Scott], chapter IV, in Woodstock; Or, The Cavalier. […], volume I, Edinburgh:  […]  [James Ballantyne and Co.] for Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Longman, Rees, Orme, Brown, and Green, →OCLC, page 120:
quote.text: […]  as the worthy dame was parcel blind and more than parcel deaf, knowledge was excluded by two principal entrances  […]

quote.citation: 1864, Alfred Tennyson, “Aylmer’s Field”, in Enoch Arden, &c., London: Edward Moxon & Co., […], →OCLC, page 59:
quote.text: here was one [a hut] that, summer-blanch’d, / Was parcel-bearded with the traveller’s-joy / In Autumn, parcel ivy-clad;
